# The Case for Remote Work as the Default for Office Jobs

The COVID-19 pandemic proved what many had long suspected: office jobs can be performed just as effectively—often more so—from home. Rather than treating remote work as a temporary accommodation, companies should embrace it as the default arrangement for office-based roles. Doing so would benefit employees, expand talent access, and generate substantial financial savings.

## Reclaiming Commute Time

The average American worker spends roughly 55 minutes per day commuting, according to U.S. Census data—amounting to nearly 240 hours per year. This time is neither compensated nor enjoyable; studies consistently link long commutes to higher stress, poorer sleep, and reduced life satisfaction. Making remote work the default returns this time to employees, who can invest it in exercise, family, hobbies, or rest. Many also use reclaimed hours to start earlier or work more focused stretches. A Stanford study led by Nicholas Bloom found remote workers were 13% more productive than their in-office counterparts, driven partly by fewer distractions and the elimination of exhausting commutes.

## Access to a Broader Talent Pool

When hiring is tethered to geography, companies limit themselves to candidates willing and able to relocate or commute to a specific office. Remote-default policies dissolve these constraints, allowing employers to recruit the best person for the role regardless of ZIP code. This is particularly valuable for specialized positions where local talent is scarce. It also promotes diversity: caregivers, people with disabilities, and workers in underserved regions gain access to opportunities previously closed to them. Companies like GitLab and Automattic, which operate fully remotely, have built world-class teams by hiring globally rather than locally.

## Financial Benefits and Reinvestment

Office space is one of the largest fixed costs for most companies. Global Workplace Analytics estimates employers save roughly $11,000 per year per half-time remote employee through reduced real estate, utilities, and overhead. Full remote-default policies multiply those savings. Rather than pocketing them, firms can reinvest in higher salaries, better benefits, and R&D that drives long-term growth.

## Conclusion

Defaulting to remote work isn't merely a perk—it's a smarter operating model. Employees gain time and well-being, companies gain talent and savings, and both are positioned to thrive.

# The Case for Remote-First Office Work

The traditional office model, built around the assumption that knowledge workers must gather daily in a central location, is a relic of an era before high-speed internet, cloud computing, and collaboration platforms. Today, office jobs should default to remote arrangements, with in-person work reserved for occasions when it delivers clear value. This shift benefits employees, employers, and the broader economy.

**Reclaiming Time from the Commute**

The average American commuter spends nearly an hour each day traveling to and from work—roughly 240 hours per year, the equivalent of six additional workweeks. Remote work returns this time to employees, who can invest it in exercise, family, sleep, or personal development. Studies from Stanford economist Nicholas Bloom have consistently shown that remote workers are not only happier but also more productive, with one landmark study of Ctrip employees documenting a 13% performance increase. Employees who begin the workday rested, rather than frazzled from traffic or crowded trains, bring sharper focus to their tasks.

**Access to a Broader Talent Pool**

When companies require employees to live within commuting distance of a headquarters, they artificially shrink their hiring pool. A New York firm competing for engineers against every other Manhattan employer pays a premium for the same talent it could recruit more affordably—and more diversely—from Cleveland, Boise, or Buenos Aires. Remote-first companies like GitLab and Automattic have built world-class teams by hiring the best candidates regardless of location. This geographic flexibility also improves representation, allowing companies to include caregivers, people with disabilities, and rural workers who are often excluded from centralized offices.

**Financial Advantages**

Commercial real estate is one of the largest fixed costs for most businesses. Global Workplace Analytics estimates that employers save around $11,000 per year for every employee who works remotely half the time. Companies going fully remote can eliminate or drastically reduce office footprints, redirecting those savings into higher salaries, R&D investment, or lower prices for customers. Dropbox and Shopify, for example, have publicly reallocated real estate budgets toward employee benefits and innovation.

**Conclusion**

Defaulting to remote work respects employees' time, widens the talent pipeline, and frees capital for more productive uses. The office should be a tool, not a requirement.

Urban public transport is often described as the circulatory system of a modern city, yet we insist on placing a toll booth at every artery. It is time to reconsider this arrangement. Making buses, trams, and metros free at the point of use would deliver profound benefits to cities and the people who live in them, transforming public transit from a grudgingly used service into a genuine public good.

The first argument for abolishing fares is a surprisingly practical one: collecting them is expensive. Ticket machines must be purchased, maintained, and repaired. Inspectors must be employed. Payment systems must be designed, secured, and continually upgraded. Anti-fraud measures, cash handling, and the administrative overhead of reconciling revenue all consume a significant portion of the money passengers pay. In some smaller networks, the cost of collection swallows nearly as much as the fares themselves generate. Redirecting these resources into more frequent services, cleaner vehicles, and better-maintained stations would give riders far more value than the fares ever did.

The second argument concerns congestion. Anyone who has sat idling in rush-hour traffic knows that our streets are choked, largely by private cars making short journeys that could easily be made by bus or tram. Price is a powerful nudge, and eliminating it would tip countless daily decisions away from the car and toward transit. Fewer vehicles on the road means faster journeys for everyone, including those who still must drive, along with cleaner air, quieter neighbourhoods, and reduced carbon emissions. Cities like Tallinn and Luxembourg have already demonstrated that free transit can meaningfully shift travel behaviour.

The third and perhaps most compelling argument is one of social justice. For low-income residents, the cost of getting to work, to a clinic, to a school, or to a job interview is not a trivial matter. Fares can consume a painful share of a modest budget, and the choice between a bus ticket and a meal is one no city dweller should have to make. Free public transport removes a persistent barrier to opportunity, connecting people to the employment, education, and services that allow them to thrive.

# In Defense of Homework: Why Primary Schools Should Not Abandon Daily Assignments

In recent years, a growing chorus of voices has called for the abolition of homework in primary schools, arguing that young children should be free to play and relax after their school day. While this sentiment is well-intentioned, it overlooks the vital role that daily homework plays in a child's academic and personal development. Far from being a burden, homework is an essential tool that reinforces classroom learning, cultivates independence, and strengthens the connection between school and home.

The most obvious benefit of daily homework is that it consolidates the reading and arithmetic skills children acquire in the classroom. A single lesson on multiplication or phonics is rarely enough for a young mind to master new material. Just as an athlete must practise regularly to perform well on the field, a child must revisit new concepts repeatedly for them to take root. A twenty-minute reading task each evening, for example, dramatically increases vocabulary and fluency over the course of a school year, while a short set of arithmetic problems helps embed number facts into long-term memory. Without this consistent reinforcement, knowledge fades quickly, and teachers must waste valuable class time reteaching material.

Beyond academic reinforcement, homework fosters the independent work habits that children will desperately need when they progress to secondary school. In the primary years, homework teaches children how to manage their time, organise their materials, and complete tasks without constant adult supervision. A pupil who has spent five or six years quietly working through evening assignments arrives at secondary school already equipped to handle longer projects and stricter deadlines. Abolishing homework would leave children unprepared for this transition, throwing them into deep water without ever having learned to swim.

Finally, homework provides a valuable window through which parents can observe their child's education. When a mother helps her son sound out words, or a father checks his daughter's sums, they gain immediate insight into what is being taught and where their child might be struggling. This partnership between home and school benefits everyone. For these reasons, primary schools should preserve, not abolish, the tradition of daily homework.

Urban public transport is one of the most vital services a city provides, yet in most places it remains locked behind a turnstile. It is time to reconsider this model and make buses, trams, and metros free at the point of use. Far from being a utopian fantasy, fare-free transit is a practical reform that would strengthen city finances, unclog our streets, and open new horizons for those who need them most.

Consider first the surprising economics of fare collection itself. Ticket machines, gates, inspectors, cash handling, card systems, and anti-fraud enforcement swallow a remarkable share of the revenue they exist to protect. In many transit networks, the cost of collecting fares consumes between a fifth and a third of the money brought in, and in some smaller systems the margin is even thinner. Every dollar spent policing turnstiles is a dollar not spent on more frequent buses, cleaner carriages, or better accessibility. Removing fares would free operators to redirect resources toward the improvements that actually attract riders.

The second argument concerns congestion. A significant portion of urban car trips are short journeys of just a few kilometres, precisely the trips public transport is best equipped to absorb. When people weigh whether to take the bus for a quick errand, even a modest fare can tip them toward the convenience of the car. Eliminate that friction, and marginal drivers become regular passengers. The result is fewer vehicles crawling through intersections, lower emissions, quieter streets, and faster journeys for everyone, including the buses themselves.

Finally, and perhaps most importantly, free transit is a matter of basic fairness. For low-income residents, the daily cost of getting to work, to a clinic, to a job interview, or to a school can be a genuine barrier. Mobility is opportunity, and pricing it out of reach entrenches inequality in the most literal geographic sense. A free network expands the labour market, connects families to services, and gives every resident an equal claim to the city.

Free public transport is not a giveaway. It is an investment in efficiency, sustainability, and equity that any modern city can afford.

# In Defense of Homework: Why Primary Schools Must Not Abandon Daily Practice

In recent years, a growing chorus of voices has called for primary schools to abolish homework, arguing that young children deserve to have their evenings entirely free from academic obligations. While this position may seem compassionate on the surface, it fails to account for the genuine educational benefits that daily homework provides. Far from being an unnecessary burden, homework is a cornerstone of primary education that reinforces essential skills, cultivates lifelong learning habits, and strengthens the vital partnership between school and home.

The most immediate value of homework lies in its power to reinforce the reading and arithmetic skills that form the foundation of a child's education. A single lesson on multiplication or a brief classroom reading session is rarely sufficient for a young learner to master new material. Neuroscientific research consistently shows that memory is strengthened through spaced repetition, meaning that a child who practises times tables for fifteen minutes each evening will retain them far more securely than one who encounters them only in class. Similarly, twenty minutes of daily reading at home dramatically expands vocabulary and fluency, giving children the confidence to tackle more complex texts as they progress through school.

Beyond academic reinforcement, homework plays a crucial role in shaping the independent work habits that children will urgently need when they enter secondary school. In secondary education, students are expected to manage multiple subjects, meet deadlines, and study without constant supervision. A child who has never learned to sit down, organise materials, and complete a task independently will find this transition overwhelming. Small, manageable homework tasks in primary school—such as completing a worksheet or writing a short paragraph—teach children self-discipline, time management, and personal responsibility in a low-stakes environment.

Finally, homework serves as an invaluable window through which parents can observe what their child is studying. Without homework, many parents would have only a vague sense of their child's curriculum or progress. Reviewing a spelling list or helping with a maths problem allows parents to identify areas of difficulty early and celebrate genuine achievements. For these reasons, abolishing homework would deprive children of essential educational support.

# Nuclear Power: An Indispensable Pillar of a Decarbonised Grid

As nations race to decarbonise their electricity systems, an ideological aversion to nuclear power threatens to undermine the very climate goals it could help achieve. A rigorous appraisal of the evidence reveals that nuclear energy is not merely a useful supplement to renewables but an indispensable component of any credible pathway to net zero.

The most compelling case for nuclear rests on its ability to provide firm, dispatchable output independent of weather conditions. Whereas wind and solar generation fluctuate with atmospheric variability—often falling to near-zero during prolonged "dunkelflaute" events in winter—nuclear reactors routinely operate at capacity factors exceeding 90%, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. This reliability is essential for maintaining grid frequency and inertia. Modelling by the MIT Energy Initiative (2018) and the IEA's *Net Zero by 2050* roadmap consistently shows that decarbonisation pathways excluding nuclear are significantly more expensive, as they require vast overbuilding of renewables and storage to compensate for intermittency. Nuclear thus complements variable renewables, forming the backbone upon which a predominantly renewable system can reliably rest.

Nuclear also compares favourably with other low-carbon technologies on lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions. The IPCC's Fifth Assessment Report attributes to nuclear a median lifecycle emission of approximately 12 gCO₂-eq/kWh—comparable to onshore wind (11 g) and considerably lower than utility-scale solar photovoltaics (roughly 48 g), whose upstream manufacturing is emissions-intensive. When mining, construction, operation, and decommissioning are all accounted for, nuclear ranks among the cleanest energy sources ever deployed at scale, having already avoided an estimated 70 gigatonnes of CO₂ emissions since 1971 (IEA, 2019).

Equally significant is nuclear's remarkable land-use efficiency. The U.S. Department of Energy calculates that a typical 1 GW nuclear plant occupies around one square mile, whereas an equivalent solar facility requires roughly 75 times more land, and wind farms up to 360 times more. In a world of competing demands for agriculture, habitat conservation, and human settlement, this spatial parsimony is a decisive ecological virtue.

Excluding nuclear from the decarbonisation toolkit is a luxury the climate cannot afford. Firm, low-carbon, and land-efficient, nuclear power is not optional—it is essential.

# Nuclear Power: The Indispensable Backbone of a Decarbonised Grid

As nations race to eliminate carbon emissions from their electricity systems, an uncomfortable truth is becoming increasingly evident: renewables alone cannot deliver a reliable, fully decarbonised grid. Nuclear power, long treated as a controversial afterthought in climate policy, is in fact an indispensable pillar of any credible net-zero strategy. Its unique combination of dispatchability, low emissions, and land efficiency makes it complementary—not antagonistic—to the expansion of wind and solar.

The most compelling case for nuclear lies in its capacity to provide firm, weather-independent baseload power. Wind and solar, while cheap and abundant, are inherently intermittent: solar farms produce nothing at night, and wind output can collapse for days during atmospheric lulls, as observed during Europe's 2021 "wind drought." Nuclear reactors, by contrast, operate at capacity factors typically exceeding 90% (IAEA, 2023), generating electricity continuously regardless of meteorological conditions. Studies by MIT's Energy Initiative (2018) demonstrate that decarbonisation pathways excluding firm low-carbon sources like nuclear cost significantly more—often two to three times higher—than those integrating it, because vast overbuilding of renewables and storage is required to compensate for variability.

Nuclear power also excels on lifecycle emissions. The IPCC's Fifth Assessment Report attributes to nuclear a median lifecycle emissions intensity of just 12 gCO₂-eq/kWh—comparable to onshore wind (11 g) and lower than solar photovoltaics (48 g). When mining, construction, fuel enrichment, and decommissioning are all accounted for, nuclear ranks among the cleanest energy sources ever deployed. Nations with historically nuclear-heavy grids, such as France and Sweden, achieved deep decarbonisation of their electricity systems decades before wind and solar became economically viable.

Finally, nuclear's land-use footprint is remarkably small. According to the U.S. Department of Energy (2022), a 1,000 MW nuclear facility occupies roughly one square mile, whereas equivalent output from solar requires around 75 times more land, and from wind approximately 360 times more. In an era of biodiversity loss and land-use competition, this compactness is a decisive ecological advantage.

A pragmatic climate strategy must therefore embrace nuclear alongside renewables. Rejecting it is not environmentalism—it is a costly ideological luxury the planet cannot afford.

# The Case Against Mandatory Age Verification on Social Media

The push for mandatory age verification on social media is well-intentioned, but the cure would prove worse than the disease. While protecting minors online is a legitimate concern, requiring every user to prove their age before participating in digital public life would erode privacy, fail to achieve its stated goals, and disproportionately harm those who can least afford it.

The most immediate casualty of age verification would be personal privacy. Verifying age reliably requires collecting sensitive documents—government IDs, biometric face scans, or credit card information—and linking them to online accounts. This creates vast new databases of identity information ripe for hacking, as demonstrated by the 2023 breach of an age verification provider used by adult websites. It also ends the possibility of anonymous or pseudonymous speech online, a protection that has historically safeguarded whistleblowers, abuse survivors, LGBTQ+ youth in hostile environments, and political dissidents. Once every social media post can be tied to a verified legal identity, the chilling effect on free expression becomes profound.

Worse, these sweeping costs would buy remarkably little protection. Tech-savvy teenagers—the very group these laws target—routinely bypass such measures using VPNs, borrowed credentials, or fake documents. Studies of similar age-gating systems, including those imposed in the United Kingdom and various U.S. states, have shown minors easily circumvent restrictions while adults bear the compliance burden. Meanwhile, the harms minors actually face online, such as cyberbullying, predatory contact, and algorithmic amplification of harmful content, are not solved by knowing a user's birthdate. They require better platform design, content moderation, and digital literacy education—not identity checks at the door.

Finally, mandatory verification imposes unequal burdens. Millions of Americans lack government-issued photo ID, disproportionately including low-income individuals, elderly citizens, and racial minorities. Requiring ID to access ordinary online communication effectively disenfranchises these groups from participation in modern civic and social life.

Protecting children is essential, but sacrificing everyone's privacy, speech, and access for a policy that demonstrably fails is not protection—it is theater. Better, more targeted solutions exist, and lawmakers should pursue them instead.

# The Case Against Mandatory Age Verification on Social Media

The impulse to shield minors from online harm is understandable, but mandatory age verification for social media accounts is a misguided policy that would create more problems than it solves. Despite its well-intentioned framing, such a mandate would erode privacy, fail to achieve its stated goal, and disproportionately harm vulnerable populations.

The most immediate consequence of mandatory age verification is the destruction of online anonymity. To confirm a user's age, platforms must collect sensitive identifying documents—government IDs, biometric facial scans, or credit card information. This creates enormous centralized databases of personal data that are irresistible targets for hackers. The 2023 breach of an age-verification provider used by adult websites exposed users' identities and browsing habits, illustrating exactly the kind of catastrophic privacy failure that awaits at scale. Even law-abiding adults would be forced to surrender anonymity that protects whistleblowers, domestic abuse survivors, LGBTQ+ individuals in hostile environments, and political dissidents.

Compounding this privacy cost is the fact that age verification simply does not work. Tech-savvy minors—precisely the population the law targets—can bypass restrictions using VPNs, borrowed credentials, or older siblings' identification. Studies of jurisdictions that have implemented similar laws, including Louisiana's age-verification requirements for adult sites, show that traffic simply migrates to non-compliant platforms rather than disappearing. The children the law claims to protect remain online; they are merely pushed toward less regulated, potentially more dangerous corners of the internet.

Finally, verification requirements impose unequal burdens across society. Roughly 11% of American adults lack government-issued photo ID, a group disproportionately composed of low-income, elderly, and minority citizens. Requiring ID to participate in social media—now a primary venue for civic discourse, job searching, and community building—effectively disenfranchises these populations from digital public life. Immigrants, unhoused individuals, and rural residents without reliable internet-connected devices face compounded barriers.

Protecting minors online is a legitimate goal, but it should be pursued through digital literacy education, better parental tools, and targeted platform design—not through surveillance mandates that sacrifice privacy, exclude the marginalized, and fail to protect the very children they invoke.

The suggestion that space-exploration funding should be siphoned off to pay for ocean research has an intuitive appeal, particularly to those who point out how little of our own seabed has been mapped in comparison to the surface of Mars. Yet the argument rests on a false premise, and closer inspection reveals that space and ocean science are not competitors for the same pot of money but complementary enterprises whose progress reinforces one another.

To begin with, the budgets that fund space agencies and those that fund oceanographic institutions are, in most countries, drawn from largely separate lines of government expenditure and are shaped by distinct political constituencies. NASA's appropriation, for instance, is set by different congressional subcommittees from those overseeing the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's marine programmes, and cutting one has historically done nothing to swell the other. The same is true of the European Space Agency and Europe's various marine research councils. A pound taken from a Mars rover is far more likely to be absorbed into general savings, defence, or unrelated programmes than to find its way into a submersible. The trade-off imagined by advocates of reallocation is therefore largely illusory, and the real competition oceanography faces comes not from space but from indifference within its own funding streams.

Moreover, space research is not the antagonist of ocean science but one of its most powerful tools. Satellite altimetry, remote sensing of sea-surface temperature, tracking of chlorophyll blooms, monitoring of sea-ice extent, and mapping of ocean currents all depend on orbital instruments that no ship or buoy network could replicate. Much of what we know about the global ocean at scale, including the mechanics of climate change, has come from space-based observation. Diminishing space capability would, paradoxically, impoverish marine science.

Finally, space programmes are unusually generative of spillover benefits, seeding advances in materials, medical imaging, telecommunications, microelectronics, water purification, and countless other fields. Few areas of public spending yield such broad downstream returns. To curtail space investment in the name of the oceans would therefore not only fail to help marine research but would forfeit gains that ripple through the wider economy.

# In Defence of Standardised Testing in University Admissions

In recent years, a growing chorus of critics has called for universities to abandon standardised tests such as the SAT and ACT as admissions criteria. While well-intentioned, this position is misguided. Standardised tests remain one of the fairest, most predictive, and most equitable tools available to admissions officers, and their removal would ultimately harm the very students reformers hope to help.

First, standardised tests provide a genuinely level playing field for applicants from vastly different educational backgrounds. A student attending an under-resourced rural school and another from an elite private academy submit transcripts that are essentially incomparable: grading scales differ, course offerings vary wildly, and an "A" at one institution may reflect entirely different levels of mastery than at another. A standardised test, by contrast, measures every applicant against the same benchmark on the same day under the same conditions. It offers talented students from lesser-known schools a concrete way to demonstrate that they can compete with peers from prestigious institutions—an opportunity they might otherwise be denied.

Second, abandoning standardised tests would paradoxically exacerbate the very inequalities critics cite. Without test scores, admissions committees rely more heavily on factors that correlate far more strongly with wealth and privilege: extracurricular activities, personal essays polished by paid consultants, letters of recommendation from well-connected teachers, and the reputational prestige of an applicant's high school. Recent research from Opportunity Insights at Harvard has shown that test scores, when contextualised, are actually better than grades at identifying high-achieving low-income students. Removing tests hands even more power to the opaque, subjective elements of admissions that wealthy families are best positioned to game.

Finally, the empirical evidence on predictive validity is compelling. While high school grades are useful, studies consistently show that standardised test scores add significant incremental predictive power for first-year university performance, particularly given the pervasive grade inflation seen at many secondary schools. Combined, tests and grades predict success better than either alone.

Rather than discarding a valuable tool, universities should use standardised tests thoughtfully and in context—preserving fairness, opportunity, and academic rigour.

The proposal to divert a significant portion of space-exploration funding to ocean research rests on an intuitive appeal to earthly priorities, but it collapses under closer scrutiny. To begin with, the premise that space and ocean science compete for the same pool of money is largely mistaken. In most countries, oceanographic research is funded through separate agencies and ministries: in the United States, for example, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the National Science Foundation draw from budget lines quite distinct from those that support NASA's exploration programmes, and similar institutional divisions exist in Europe and Asia. Marine science is not underfunded because astronauts are funded; it is underfunded because governments have chosen not to prioritise it within its own budgetary sphere. Framing the two as substitutes obscures the real political question, which is why ocean science struggles to attract the direct investment it deserves.

Moreover, space research is not the rival of oceanography but one of its most powerful enablers. A vast proportion of what we know about the oceans today comes from orbital observation: satellite altimetry maps sea-surface topography and currents, radiometers track temperature and salinity, and imaging instruments monitor plankton blooms, ice extent, and pollution on scales no ship-based survey could ever approach. Missions such as Jason, Sentinel, and SWOT have transformed climate and marine science. Stripping funds from space programmes would, paradoxically, weaken the very infrastructure on which modern oceanography depends, leaving marine researchers with fewer tools rather than more.

Finally, space programmes generate an unusually broad range of spillover benefits into other industries, benefits that would be difficult to replicate through investment in any single field. The technologies developed for exploration have seeded advances in medical imaging, materials science, telecommunications, weather forecasting, water purification, and computing, with returns that studies consistently estimate at several times the original public expenditure. Ocean research, valuable as it is, cannot claim a comparable record of cross-sectoral innovation. Rather than cannibalising a programme whose economic and scientific dividends are exceptionally wide, a sensible policy would expand ocean funding on its own merits while preserving the distinctive engine of discovery that space exploration provides.

# In Defence of Standardised Testing in University Admissions

In recent years, a growing chorus of voices has called for universities to abandon standardised tests as a factor in admissions decisions. While well-intentioned, this position overlooks the crucial role these assessments play in ensuring fair, informed, and equitable admissions. Far from being obstacles to opportunity, standardised tests remain one of the most reliable tools available to admissions officers.

First, a common standardised test provides a level playing field for applicants from vastly diverse educational backgrounds. Students apply to universities from thousands of different high schools, each with its own curriculum, grading standards, and academic culture. An "A" at one school may reflect achievement well below a "B" at another. Standardised tests offer a single, uniform benchmark against which all applicants can be measured, allowing a talented student from an under-resourced rural school to demonstrate their abilities on equal terms with a peer from an elite private academy. Without such a benchmark, admissions officers are left comparing apples to oranges.

Second, the absence of standardised testing would, paradoxically, exacerbate existing inequalities in the admissions process. When tests are removed, admissions committees rely more heavily on factors that correlate even more strongly with wealth: polished personal essays, expensive extracurricular activities, glowing recommendation letters from well-connected teachers, and unpaid internships. Affluent families can purchase these advantages, whereas a high test score achieved through hard work and a modest preparation book cannot easily be bought. Recent research from MIT and other institutions that reinstated testing requirements found that scores helped identify high-achieving disadvantaged students who might otherwise have been overlooked.

Finally, standardised tests possess strong predictive validity for first-year university success, often rivalling or exceeding that of high school grades. Studies conducted by the College Board and independent researchers consistently show that test scores predict first-year GPA, retention, and graduation rates. Because grades vary in meaning across schools, their predictive power weakens without a standardised anchor; combining the two yields the most accurate forecasts of all.

For these reasons, abandoning standardised testing would harm the very students reformers hope to help. Universities should retain—not discard—this valuable admissions tool.

# The Case for a Four-Day Working Week

The way we work is overdue for reform. The five-day, forty-hour week is not a law of nature but a relic of the industrial age, designed for factory floors rather than knowledge economies and modern service industries. It is time for our government to be bold and adopt the four-day working week as national policy. Far from being a utopian indulgence, a shorter week would boost productivity, safeguard the health of the workforce, and open up new opportunities for employment across the country.

The most persuasive evidence comes from the trials that have already taken place. In the largest British pilot, involving sixty-one companies and nearly three thousand workers, an overwhelming majority reported that output was maintained or even improved despite the reduction in hours. Similar results have been recorded in Iceland, Belgium and Japan, where firms such as Microsoft saw productivity jump by around forty per cent. When employees know they have one fewer day to complete their work, meetings become shorter, distractions are minimised, and time is used with far greater discipline. In short, we have moved beyond speculation: the evidence shows that a compressed week does not compress performance.

A four-day week would also produce a healthier, more resilient workforce. Chronic overwork is one of the biggest drivers of stress, burnout and long-term sickness absence, which currently costs the British economy tens of billions of pounds each year. When workers are given a genuine third day to rest, exercise, see family and attend medical appointments, they return to their desks recharged rather than depleted. Trial after trial has recorded sharp falls in reported stress and sick days taken, easing pressure not only on employers but on an overstretched health service.

Finally, a shorter week would help spread work more evenly across society. If existing hours are redistributed, employers will need to recruit additional staff to cover demand, creating openings for the unemployed and the underemployed. In an age of automation and precarious contracts, sharing the available work more fairly is not just economically sensible but morally right. The four-day week is an idea whose time has come.

# The Case for a Four-Day Working Week

The traditional five-day working week is a relic of an industrial era that bears little resemblance to the modern economy. As nations grapple with burnout, stagnant productivity, and persistent unemployment, it is time to embrace a bold but evidence-based reform: adopting the four-day working week as national policy. Far from being a utopian fantasy, this shift promises to sustain economic output, improve public health, and distribute work more fairly across society.

Critics often assume that fewer hours must mean less production, but the evidence firmly contradicts this instinct. Large-scale trials, most notably the landmark UK pilot involving thousands of employees across dozens of companies, have demonstrated that output can be maintained, and in many cases improved, when the working week is shortened. Freed from the tyranny of unnecessary meetings and low-value tasks, workers become more focused, more efficient, and more engaged during the hours they do work. Iceland's nationwide experiment reached similar conclusions, revealing that productivity per hour rises when workers are not stretched thin. The lesson is clear: hours worked and value created are not the same thing.

Equally compelling is the impact on workforce health. Chronic overwork is one of the leading drivers of stress, anxiety, and physical illness, and the resulting sick leave costs employers billions each year. A well-rested workforce is a resilient workforce. When employees are given a genuine chance to recover, exercise, spend time with loved ones, and attend to personal responsibilities, they return to work healthier and more motivated. The trials that have already been conducted show measurable drops in sick days and reported burnout, translating directly into savings for businesses and less strain on public health services.

Finally, a shorter working week offers a powerful tool for tackling unemployment. By spreading the available work across more people, employers would need to recruit additional staff to cover reduced individual hours, creating fresh opportunities for those currently locked out of the labour market. This redistribution of work would ease inequality, reduce welfare dependency, and inject new energy into local economies. The four-day week is not merely desirable; it is overdue.

Banning private cars from city centres is one of the most transformative urban policies available to modern municipalities. Far from being a punitive measure against motorists, it is a rational reallocation of scarce public space that delivers measurable benefits in liveability, public health, and economic vitality. The evidence from cities that have taken this step is compelling, and the arguments in its favour deserve serious consideration.

The most immediate gain is the liberation of street space for uses that serve far more people than private vehicles ever could. A single traffic lane occupied by cars moving one or two passengers at a time can, once reclaimed, accommodate wide pedestrian promenades, protected cycle lanes, tram corridors, outdoor seating, street markets, and public greenery. Oslo, which removed most on-street parking from its centre, converted these spaces into plazas, bike lanes, and expanded pavements, transforming previously congested streets into places where people linger rather than merely pass through. Space is finite in dense urban cores, and dedicating the majority of it to storing and moving private cars is an indefensible use of a precious civic resource.

The environmental improvements that follow such bans are neither speculative nor slow to materialise. When Madrid restricted private cars from its central district in 2018, nitrogen dioxide levels fell by around 15 percent within months. Paris and Brussels have documented similar declines in both air pollutants and ambient noise following pedestrianisation schemes. Reductions in noise pollution, often overlooked, yield real benefits for cardiovascular health, sleep quality, and cognitive performance among residents. These improvements accrue quickly precisely because the largest single source of central-city pollution — combustion-engine traffic — is simply removed.

Perhaps most surprising to sceptics is the consistent finding that retail footfall rises after such bans. Studies in Copenhagen, Madrid, and numerous German cities show that pedestrians and cyclists, though they may spend less per visit, visit more frequently and cumulatively outspend drivers. Shopkeepers routinely overestimate the share of their customers arriving by car. When streets become pleasant environments to walk and dwell in, people stay longer and spend more. Banning private cars is therefore not just an environmental policy but a proven engine of urban economic renewal.

# In Defence of the Modern Zoo

The proposal to phase out zoos, though well-intentioned, misunderstands the vital role these institutions play in the modern conservation landscape. Far from being outdated relics of Victorian curiosity, today's zoos are sophisticated centres of science, education, and species preservation. To abolish them would be to dismantle one of the most effective tools we possess in the fight against biodiversity loss.

Consider first the extraordinary contribution of zoo-based breeding programmes, which have rescued numerous species from the brink of extinction. The Arabian oryx, declared extinct in the wild in 1972, was reintroduced to its native deserts entirely through the efforts of coordinated zoo breeding initiatives, and now roams freely once more across the Arabian Peninsula. Similarly, the California condor, whose global population dwindled to just twenty-seven individuals in the 1980s, has been brought back from near-oblivion through captive breeding at institutions such as San Diego Zoo. The Przewalski's horse, the golden lion tamarin, and the Amur leopard owe their continued existence to genetic management strategies that would be impossible without a network of accredited zoological institutions working in concert.

Equally significant is the role zoos play in cultivating public support for conservation. Documentaries and books, however compelling, cannot replicate the visceral experience of meeting a living animal face to face. When a child stands before a tiger and feels the weight of its gaze, or watches an orangutan cradle its infant, an emotional connection is forged that no screen can replicate. This connection translates into tangible conservation outcomes: zoo visitors are demonstrably more likely to donate to wildlife charities, support environmental legislation, and adopt sustainable behaviours in their own lives. Without such encounters, public engagement with distant ecological crises would inevitably wane.

Finally, veterinary research conducted within zoos has yielded discoveries that directly benefit wild populations. Advances in wildlife anaesthesia, vaccine development for diseases such as canine distemper in African wild dogs, and improved understanding of reproductive physiology have all emerged from zoo-based science. Field veterinarians treating injured or diseased wild animals routinely rely upon protocols pioneered in zoological settings. Phasing out zoos would therefore not liberate wildlife; it would deprive it of some of its most dedicated defenders.

# In Defence of the Modern Zoo

Calls to phase out zoos have grown louder in recent years, driven by an understandable concern for animal welfare. Yet such proposals, however well-intentioned, fail to reckon with the indispensable contributions that modern zoological institutions make to global conservation. Far from being relics of a less enlightened age, today's zoos are scientific centres whose closure would represent a devastating blow to wildlife worldwide.

The most compelling case for zoos lies in their extraordinary success as breeding sanctuaries for species on the brink of extinction. The Arabian oryx, hunted to extinction in the wild by 1972, was reintroduced to its native deserts entirely thanks to a captive breeding programme initiated at Phoenix Zoo. Similarly, the California condor, whose wild population had collapsed to just twenty-two individuals in the 1980s, now numbers over five hundred birds because of coordinated zoo-led recovery efforts. The Przewalski's horse, the Père David's deer, and the golden lion tamarin owe their continued existence to the same institutions that critics propose to dismantle. Without zoos, these species would exist only in photographs.

Equally important is the role that direct encounters with animals play in cultivating public support for conservation. Documentaries and virtual experiences, valuable as they are, cannot replicate the visceral impact of standing before a living tiger or watching a gorilla cradle her infant. Studies consistently show that visitors leave zoos with heightened environmental awareness and greater willingness to donate to conservation causes. Children in particular develop emotional bonds with wildlife through zoo visits, and it is these bonds that produce the next generation of scientists, campaigners, and voters who will defend natural habitats. Sever this connection, and public engagement with biodiversity loss will inevitably wither.

Finally, veterinary research undertaken within zoos has yielded discoveries that benefit wild populations far beyond their gates. Techniques for anaesthetising large mammals, developed in zoos, are now routinely used by field biologists tagging free-ranging animals. Vaccines against canine distemper, protocols for treating avian malaria, and advances in reproductive technology all originated in zoo laboratories.

To phase out zoos would be to abandon the very institutions that stand between many species and oblivion.

In an age when a tap of a phone or a swipe of a card can settle almost any transaction, it is tempting to imagine that physical cash has outlived its purpose. Yet the very ubiquity of digital payment systems is precisely what makes the continued circulation of banknotes and coins so essential. Far from being a relic of a bygone economy, cash remains a quietly indispensable pillar of a resilient, inclusive, and free society, and its erosion would carry consequences that extend well beyond mere inconvenience.

The first and perhaps most tangible virtue of cash lies in its resilience during infrastructural failure. Digital payments depend on an intricate lattice of electricity, internet connectivity, functioning servers, and operational point-of-sale terminals. When any link in this chain breaks — whether through a storm-induced power outage, a cyberattack on a banking network, or a simple software glitch — commerce grinds to a halt. Cash, by contrast, requires no signal and no socket. In moments of crisis, from natural disasters to geopolitical shocks, it is the physical note in the pocket that keeps bread on the table and fuel in the tank, offering a fail-safe that no server farm can guarantee.

A second consideration, no less profound, concerns privacy. Cash is the only payment instrument that leaves no digital footprint. Every card swipe, mobile transfer, or contactless tap generates data that can be aggregated, analysed, monetised, or, in more troubling scenarios, surveilled by corporations or states. Cash preserves the citizen's right to conduct lawful transactions without their habits, preferences, and movements being catalogued, safeguarding a sphere of personal autonomy that is increasingly rare in the modern world.

Finally, cash remains a lifeline for those whom the digital economy leaves behind. The unbanked, who lack access to formal financial institutions, and many elderly people, who may find smartphones and online banking bewildering or inaccessible, rely on physical currency for their daily needs. To abandon cash is to disenfranchise them.

For these reasons — resilience, privacy, and inclusion — a robust circulation of cash must be actively preserved.

Banning private cars from city centres is one of the most transformative urban policies available to modern municipalities. Far from being a punitive restriction on mobility, it is a liberating reallocation of scarce urban space, delivering measurable gains in public health, environmental quality, and even the commercial vitality that opponents claim it would undermine. The case for such a ban rests on three powerful and mutually reinforcing arguments.

First, removing private vehicles unlocks vast quantities of street space for uses that serve people rather than machines. In most historic city centres, roads and parking consume more than half of all public land, yet they are used by a small minority of citizens at any given moment. Reclaiming this space allows for generous pedestrian boulevards, protected cycling networks, outdoor seating for cafés and restaurants, pocket parks, and public plazas where cultural life can flourish. Streets cease to be conduits for through-traffic and become genuine civic spaces, hosting markets, performances, and the informal encounters that constitute urban life. Cities such as Pontevedra, Ghent, and Oslo have demonstrated how quickly asphalt can be reimagined as habitat once the car is displaced.

Second, the empirical evidence for rapid environmental improvement is striking. In Madrid's central low-emission zone, nitrogen dioxide concentrations fell by roughly 20 percent within a year of implementation, while Paris recorded comparable reductions along the Seine embankments after their pedestrianisation. Noise levels, measured in decibels, typically drop by five to ten points on formerly trafficked streets—a difference perceived by the human ear as roughly a halving of loudness. These are not gradual, generational shifts but changes registered within months, translating directly into fewer respiratory illnesses, better sleep, and lower cardiovascular stress for residents.

Finally, and counterintuitively, retail thrives rather than withers. Studies from Copenhagen, New York's Times Square, and multiple German pedestrianised zones consistently show footfall increases of 20 to 40 percent following car bans, with corresponding rises in shop turnover. Merchants habitually overestimate the share of customers arriving by car and underestimate the appetite of pedestrians and cyclists to linger and spend. Banning private cars is thus not merely defensible but demonstrably beneficial across every relevant dimension of urban life.

# Why Universal Programming Instruction at Six Is the Wrong Path

In recent years, an enthusiastic chorus of technologists and policymakers has insisted that every child should begin learning to code at the age of six. While the intentions behind this proposal are understandable, the idea deserves far more scrutiny than it has received. Introducing formal programming into the earliest years of schooling risks displacing more valuable learning, chasing skills that will not last, and overburdening a teaching workforce that is not equipped to deliver it.

The early years of a child's education are far better spent building a strong foundation in language, number sense, and imaginative play. These are the years in which the brain is uniquely primed to absorb vocabulary, develop phonemic awareness, and grasp the basic logic of quantity and pattern. Imaginative play, meanwhile, is not a frivolous pastime but the very engine through which young children develop empathy, social reasoning, and creative problem-solving. Squeezing structured coding lessons into a six-year-old's day inevitably means squeezing out storytelling, building blocks, and outdoor exploration—precisely the experiences that research consistently shows to be irreplaceable at that age.

Even setting aside developmental concerns, there is a practical problem: the tools and languages that dominate programming today may bear little resemblance to those used a decade from now. The pace of change in software is relentless. A child taught the syntax of a particular block-based platform at age six will find, by the time they are old enough to apply those skills in any meaningful context, that the industry has moved on. Teaching computational thinking through age-appropriate activities later in schooling produces far more durable results than front-loading technical instruction that quickly becomes obsolete.

Finally, the shortage of qualified computing teachers makes universal high-quality coding instruction an unrealistic promise. Schools across the country already struggle to recruit specialists, and a mandate that stretches instruction down to the youngest grades would only spread scarce expertise thinner. The likely outcome is not uniform excellence but uneven, superficial teaching that could sour children on the very subject we hope to inspire them to love.

In recent years, a chorus of technologists, policymakers, and well-meaning parents has grown increasingly loud in its insistence that every child should begin learning to program by the age of six. While the intention behind this proposal is understandable in an era shaped by digital transformation, the argument overlooks important truths about childhood development, the volatile nature of technology, and the practical realities of our schools. Mandating programming instruction for all six-year-olds is not only unnecessary; it is likely to do more harm than good.

The early years of a child's education are best spent laying a broad and durable foundation, not narrowing the curriculum around a single technical skill. At six, children are still developing essential competencies in language, number sense, and imaginative play. Reading fluency, vocabulary, storytelling, and basic mathematical intuition are the cognitive bedrock on which all later learning, including programming, ultimately rests. Imaginative play, meanwhile, teaches children how to solve problems, cooperate with others, and think abstractly. Displacing these vital activities with syntax rules and coding exercises risks producing children who can drag blocks across a screen but who lack the richer intellectual scaffolding that makes real innovation possible.

There is also the matter of technological obsolescence. Programming languages, frameworks, and tools evolve at a dizzying pace; what is cutting-edge today is often deprecated within a decade. A six-year-old who painstakingly learns a particular platform may find, by the time she is old enough to apply that knowledge professionally, that the industry has moved on entirely. Teaching core reasoning skills, by contrast, produces adaptable thinkers who can pick up whatever tools the future demands.

Finally, we must reckon with the practical constraints facing our schools. There is already a severe shortage of teachers qualified to deliver rigorous computer science instruction, and even wealthy districts struggle to staff their programs adequately. To impose a universal coding mandate on six-year-olds would guarantee wildly uneven quality, deepening educational inequality rather than reducing it. Before we insist that every child learn to code, we should ensure that every child can first learn to read, reason, and dream.

# La gratuidad del transporte público urbano: una apuesta por la ciudad del futuro

El transporte público urbano constituye la columna vertebral de la movilidad en las ciudades contemporáneas. Frente al debate sobre su financiamiento, sostengo que su gratuidad representa una política pública de alto impacto económico, ambiental y social, cuyos beneficios superan ampliamente los costos que implica.

En primer lugar, es necesario cuestionar el mito de que cobrar tarifas resulta económicamente eficiente. La recaudación implica una infraestructura considerable: máquinas expendedoras, sistemas de validación, personal de fiscalización, mantenimiento tecnológico y campañas contra la evasión. Diversos estudios estiman que entre un 15% y un 30% de los ingresos por tarifas se destinan a los propios costos de recaudación. Eliminar este sistema no solo simplificaría la operación, sino que también agilizaría los tiempos de abordaje, reduciendo demoras y optimizando la eficiencia de las flotas. En este sentido, la gratuidad no es un gasto adicional, sino una redistribución inteligente de recursos ya existentes, complementada con financiamiento vía impuestos progresivos.

En segundo lugar, la gratuidad tendría un efecto transformador sobre los patrones de movilidad urbana. Al eliminar la barrera del costo, muchos usuarios que hoy realizan viajes cortos en automóvil optarían por el transporte público, especialmente cuando la percepción de "gratuidad inmediata" compite con el gasto en combustible y estacionamiento. Ciudades como Tallin, en Estonia, o Dunkerque, en Francia, han demostrado incrementos significativos en el uso del transporte colectivo tras implementar esta política. La consecuencia directa es una reducción de la congestión vehicular, menor emisión de gases contaminantes y una mejora tangible en la calidad del aire urbano.

Finalmente, la dimensión social resulta decisiva. Para los sectores de menores ingresos, el costo del transporte puede representar hasta el 20% del presupuesto familiar, condicionando el acceso al empleo, la educación y la salud. La gratuidad democratiza la ciudad, ampliando el radio de oportunidades para quienes hoy están geográficamente segregados por razones económicas. Se trata, en definitiva, de reconocer la movilidad como un derecho.

Adoptar la gratuidad del transporte público es apostar por ciudades más eficientes, sostenibles e inclusivas: una inversión en el bien común.

**El trabajo a distancia: una modalidad que beneficia a todos**

En las últimas décadas, la manera de entender el trabajo de oficina ha experimentado una transformación profunda. La pandemia demostró que muchas de las tareas que antes se realizaban en un cubículo pueden ejecutarse con igual o mayor eficacia desde casa. Por ello, defiendo con firmeza que el trabajo a distancia debería consolidarse como la modalidad habitual para los empleos de oficina, pues sus beneficios superan con creces a los inconvenientes.

En primer lugar, conviene reflexionar sobre el tiempo que millones de trabajadores dedican cada día a desplazarse. Una hora y media de trayecto diario equivale a casi un mes completo al año perdido entre atascos y transporte público saturado. Ese tiempo, recuperado gracias al teletrabajo, puede destinarse a actividades que enriquecen la vida personal y profesional: practicar deporte, cuidar de los hijos, formarse en nuevas competencias o simplemente descansar. Un empleado que llega a su jornada laboral con energía y equilibrio emocional rinde mejor, comete menos errores y aporta mayor creatividad a su equipo.

En segundo lugar, las empresas obtienen una ventaja competitiva innegable al eliminar las barreras geográficas en la contratación. Este acceso ampliado al talento no solo mejora la calidad de las plantillas, sino que además favorece la diversidad de perspectivas culturales y profesionales, un ingrediente clave para innovar en mercados cada vez más globales.

Por último, no puede ignorarse el impacto económico del ahorro en infraestructura. Mantener oficinas amplias, con sus correspondientes alquileres, suministros, mobiliario y servicios de limpieza, supone un desembolso enorme. Al reducir estos costes, las compañías disponen de recursos adicionales para lo verdaderamente importante: pagar mejores salarios a sus empleados o invertir en investigación y desarrollo, motores del progreso a largo plazo.

En definitiva, el teletrabajo no es una simple moda pasajera, sino una fórmula racional que dignifica al trabajador, fortalece a la empresa y contribuye al bienestar colectivo. Adoptarlo como norma no es solo deseable: es, sencillamente, lo más sensato.

# La importancia de mantener las tareas para casa en la educación primaria

En los últimos años, el debate sobre la conveniencia de eliminar las tareas escolares en la etapa de primaria ha cobrado fuerza en numerosos centros educativos. Si bien es cierto que un exceso de deberes puede resultar contraproducente, suprimirlos por completo sería un error. Las tareas para casa, cuando se plantean con criterio y en una cantidad razonable, constituyen una herramienta pedagógica valiosa que conviene preservar. A continuación, expondré tres razones fundamentales que justifican su mantenimiento.

En primer lugar, las tareas para casa permiten consolidar los conocimientos adquiridos en el aula. Durante las clases, los alumnos reciben una gran cantidad de información en un tiempo limitado, y no siempre logran asimilarla en profundidad. Al enfrentarse solos a ejercicios similares en casa, tienen la oportunidad de repasar los contenidos, detectar sus dudas y afianzar lo aprendido. Por ejemplo, un niño que practica operaciones matemáticas por la tarde interioriza mucho mejor los procedimientos que si únicamente los ve una vez en el aula. La repetición espaciada, como demuestran numerosos estudios pedagógicos, es clave para el aprendizaje duradero.

En segundo lugar, las tareas escolares preparan a los alumnos para la educación secundaria. El paso de primaria al instituto supone un salto considerable en cuanto a exigencia académica, autonomía y responsabilidad. Si los niños llegan a esa etapa sin haber desarrollado hábitos de estudio, gestión del tiempo o esfuerzo personal, se enfrentarán a serias dificultades. Realizar deberes de forma habitual, aunque sea con tareas breves y adaptadas a su edad, les enseña a organizarse, a cumplir con plazos y a asumir compromisos, competencias imprescindibles para su futuro académico.

En tercer lugar, los deberes favorecen la implicación de los padres en el proceso de aprendizaje de sus hijos. Sentarse junto al niño para revisar sus ejercicios, resolver dudas o simplemente interesarse por lo que ha aprendido en el colegio fortalece el vínculo familiar y transmite la importancia del estudio. Además, permite a las familias detectar dificultades tempranas y colaborar estrechamente con los docentes.

En conclusión, las tareas para casa, planteadas con equilibrio, son una pieza esencial de la formación integral de los niños. Eliminarlas empobrecería el proceso educativo y perjudicaría, a largo plazo, a los propios alumnos.

# La importancia de mantener las tareas en casa en la educación primaria
